evals.prompt: I run NovaData Live, a fully online two-day data engineering conference (about 3,100 registrations last year). The organizers of PipelineCon, an in-person conference in Denver with a very similar audience, are open to cross-promoting with us. Our next edition is 7 weeks out. My current idea: we each get a booth at the other's event, and we give their community a 40% discount code (our public early-bird is 20% off). Both of us can issue codes and see redemptions in our ticketing platforms. Lay out the promo plan and rank what we should do first.
evals.expected_output: A ranked cross-promotion plan that deletes the booth exchange outright (one event is online-only), leads with cross-listing plus mention/ticket-code swaps, corrects the discount depth, excludes co-location for this edition, and wires attribution before launch with self-set targets.
expectations: The booth or flyer exchange is removed from the plan entirely because one event has no physical edition, not ranked lower or deferred to later.
The ruled-out booth exchange does not reappear anywhere in the response as a bottom-ranked, future, or 'maybe later' option.
Calendar cross-listing is included as a near-free baseline action that needs no partner consent and is done regardless of the deal.
The 40% code is flagged as deeper than the event's own 20% public early-bird discount, undercutting the pricing ladder and training both communities to wait for codes.
Any recommended discount depth (such as a 15-25% range) is presented as a self-set choice, not as an industry standard.
The discount code carries an expiry and optionally a redemption cap to bound revenue exposure.
Co-location or a shared conference week is excluded for this edition because venue and dates lock 9-12 months out, far beyond the 7-week window.
Attribution (per-partner codes, campaign-tagged links, or a registration source field) is set up before launch, not reconstructed afterward.
The mention swap and/or ticket-discount swap lead the plan as the first active formats, ahead of higher-effort formats.
No invented redemption or referral benchmark figures appear; any numeric target is labeled self-set.

evals.prompt: I organize TinyTypes, a monthly TypeScript meetup in Manchester with a 900-subscriber newsletter and about 120 attendees per session. StaticLand Conf is a 2,500-attendee annual conference with a 28,000-subscriber newsletter, and our audiences overlap heavily. Write the outreach email to their lead organizer proposing we each mention the other once in our newsletters.
evals.expected_output: An organizer-to-organizer outreach email that names the size asymmetry openly and rebalances the deal in units (more mentions, richer placement, or a discount window from the smaller side), with one specific observed overlap, one concrete proposal, and a yes/no ask.
expectations: The response flags that one mention each is a bad trade for the much larger side given the roughly 30x newsletter size gap.
The proposal is rebalanced in units, not kind: the smaller side offers more mentions, a richer placement, a longer or deeper discount window, or on-site visibility.
The size asymmetry is named openly inside the outreach message itself rather than left unmentioned.
The email opens with a one-line description of who the sender is and cites a specific observed audience overlap, not a generic compliment.
The email contains exactly one concrete swap proposal, with no vague partnership language such as exploring synergies.
The email closes with a single ask answerable with yes or no.
The email is written peer-to-peer as a fellow organizer referencing the partner event's actual content, not as a vendor-to-prospect pitch.
No money, commission, or paid placement is offered; the exchange is visibility only.
The response recommends checking for a warm organizer connection or shared community space before sending the cold email.

evals.prompt: We run RustDays, a 350-person Rust conference in Lyon. RustForge in Paris is about four times our size and covers the same topics for the same crowd - most people in the community pick one of the two each year. Their audience is exactly ours, so we're thinking of moving our next edition to Paris during their week and pitching them a joint promotion push. Good idea?
evals.expected_output: A refusal grounded in the complement/substitute test: the candidate is a substitute, so the answer is to load-balance dates away from it rather than co-locate or swap, and to look for complementary events as partners instead.
expectations: The response applies a complement-versus-substitute test and identifies the other conference as a substitute, since attendees pick one of the two rather than attending both.
It advises against sharing the week, because co-locating with a substitute cannibalizes both events.
It recommends load-balancing dates away from the substitute's edition instead of moving toward it.
It declines to propose any swap (mentions, codes, joint push) with the substitute, treating it as a competitor rather than a swap partner.
It points to complementary events - including local events outside the Rust niche sharing a city or window - as the right co-location or piggyback candidates.
Audience fit is presented as the screen that can single-handedly disqualify a candidate, applied before any outreach.
It notes a co-location decision is locked to the edition cycle roughly 9-12 months out, not decided in a marketing sprint.

evals.prompt: MicroServe Day is our 220-person one-day community event on microservices. OrbitalCon, a 12,000-attendee cloud vendor conference, happens in Amsterdam every May and a lot of our crowd flies in for it. We want to hold MicroServe Day in Amsterdam the day before OrbitalCon opens, brand ourselves 'the official OrbitalCon fringe event' on our site, and ideally merge our registration into theirs so people sign up in one place. There's also apparently a paid program to get listed on their site. How should we play this?
evals.expected_output: A plan that keeps the permissionless scheduling play (day-before, same city), keeps registration separate, drops the 'official' branding pending trademark sign-off while allowing factual date references, and treats any published slot fee as one program's model to be confirmed, not a universal rate.
expectations: The response states that scheduling the day before the anchor in the same city needs no permission from the anchor and is an established organizer practice, since traveling attendees justify one trip for both events.
It advises against merging registration: co-located events keep separate registration, and clustering never requires merging ticketing or revenue.
It rejects the 'official OrbitalCon fringe event' branding, because using the anchor's name beyond factual date references may require their sign-off.
It allows a factual date reference in positioning (such as 'the day before OrbitalCon, same city') without any agreement.
It notes the no-deal route earns no reciprocity from the anchor - permissionless but one-sided.
Any figure cited for a paid co-location slot (such as a documented add-on package at one large ecosystem program) is treated as one confirmed model, not a universal rate.
It advises confirming or negotiating the anchor program's own terms explicitly - the slot fee and whether cross-promotion is included - rather than assuming either.
It confirms the anchor is a complement whose attendees would attend both events before committing to the shared week.
No invented attendee-crossover or conversion figures appear.

evals.prompt: Time to debrief the partnership between our CodeHarbor Conf and GreenStack Summit. They gave us two newsletter mentions and a shout-out from their main stage; we handed out their flyers at our registration desk and posted about them once on social. We never set up discount codes or tracking links. Write up the debrief for our organizing committee, including how many of our 1,400 registrations the partnership drove - I've read cross-promotion typically drives 5-10% of event registrations, so we can work from that.
evals.expected_output: A debrief that refuses to estimate registrations for unattributed channels, records every deliverable as unmeasured in a two-way ledger, answers the two relationship questions, closes with a recur/renegotiate/drop decision told to the partner, and mandates attribution before the next launch.
expectations: The debrief does not attribute any registration count to the partnership and produces no estimated figure for the unattributed channels.
The claimed 5-10% industry figure is rejected, on the grounds that no industry-wide measured referral value for event-to-event swaps has been published.
Deliverables with no attributable result are recorded explicitly as unmeasured, never as estimated numbers.
The debrief includes a per-partner delivery ledger covering both directions, with dates and evidence links for each deliverable.
The debrief asks the two relationship questions: was the collaboration easy, and do both sides want to recur.

First-swap success is framed modestly - both sides delivered what was agreed and the measured record becomes the baseline for the next edition - with relationship durability weighted over single-edition yield.
The debrief ends with a recur, renegotiate, or drop decision that is communicated to the partner.
The response prescribes attribution before launch for the next edition: per-partner codes, campaign-tagged links, or a registration source field.

evals.prompt: KernelFest is our volunteer-run 600-person Linux conference. ObservaCon is a commercial conference run by Metricly, a vendor that sells observability tooling. Their marketing lead and I agreed in a Slack DM to give each other a free booth at our next editions - she said 'sounds good, we'll sort the details later.' One complication I'm not sure matters: TraceHound pays us $8,000 as gold sponsor and their contract mentions something about being our exclusive observability sponsor. Also our volunteer crew is stretched and I doubt anyone can travel to staff a booth at their event. What do we need to nail down before this goes ahead?
evals.expected_output: A hold on the booth swap until the paying sponsor's category exclusivity is checked, a real written agreement replacing the Slack recap because one side is company-run, the full agreement contents (deliverables, minimums, exit clause, costs, approvals, attribution, number sharing), engagement quality as a hard gate for this expensive format, and a trade-down to flyers or a stage mention given the unstaffable booth.
expectations: The TraceHound exclusivity clause is checked against the signed sponsor agreement before any floor space is promised, flagged as the gating step.
The comped booth for Metricly, an observability vendor, is identified as in-kind value that can violate the paying sponsor's category exclusivity.
The response does not greenlight the booth swap as agreed; it holds or reshapes the deal until the exclusivity conflict is resolved.
Because one side is company-run, the Slack recap is ruled insufficient: a real written agreement is required, since informal recaps don't survive a marketing-team handover.
The timeline is set to the slower company-side approval chain, anticipating brand approval and a legal pass.
The agreement lists each side's deliverables with dates and minimum commitments.
The agreement includes an exit clause letting either side withdraw promotion, with takedown of scheduled mentions, on cancellation, material change, or a conduct incident.
The agreement names any costs explicitly, such as shipping or booth furniture, so the free swap doesn't silently accrete costs.
The agreement covers logo, event-name, and copy approvals.
The agreement covers attribution handling and commits both sides to sharing resulting numbers after the edition.
Engagement quality is escalated to a hard gate for this expensive format: real numbers such as open rates and past swap results are requested during the deal conversation.
Given the unstaffable booth, the response recommends trading the booth down to a flyer exchange or stage mention rather than running an unstaffed booth.

evals.prompt: DevSummit Porto just closed its CFP with 240 submissions for 40 slots. The organizer of CodeCoast Lisbon, which runs three months after us with a similar audience, asked if we'd send over our strong rejected talks so she can fill her program, and she'd do the same for us next cycle. Before I say yes, set this up properly and give me a registration target so I can show the committee what this earns us.
evals.expected_output: A speaker-pipeline setup gated on per-speaker consent, an explicit refusal to attach a registration target to this format (its value is program quality and goodwill, reported as unmeasured), framed as a compounding edition-over-edition play with companion forms like cross-announced CFP windows.
expectations: Speaker consent is required before forwarding any rejected CFP submission - a submission is not the organizer's to hand to a third party unasked.

The response declines to set a registration target for speaker-pipeline sharing: its value lands in program quality and speaker-community goodwill, not attributable registrations, and the debrief should say so instead of forcing a number.
Speaker-pipeline sharing is framed as a compounding, edition-over-edition play suited to a recurring relationship.
Companion forms are proposed: cross-announcing each other's CFP windows and/or directly recommending proven speakers.
No invented registration or conversion figure appears anywhere in the response.
Deliveries are tracked in the per-partner ledger with the result recorded as unmeasured rather than estimated.
